name: Eyelash growth serum (peptide, OTC)

lead: Peptide lash serums are over-the-counter products applied to the lash line, aimed at longer, thicker, fuller lashes that frame the eyes. They are often positioned as non-prescription alternatives to prescription bimatoprost (Latisse), a prostaglandin analogue.

Lashes differ from scalp hair: their length is largely genetically set, follicle number cannot increase after birth, and length, thickness and darkness decline with age. Some brands use peptides instead of prostaglandins because of regulatory rules in places such as Canada and California. No published human trials of the peptide products were found; trial data exist for bimatoprost.

paras: The serum is brushed along the base of the lashes, usually daily over weeks. Forum users ask for brand recommendations, report mixed results, and compare it with castor oil, rosemary oil, minoxidil and Latisse.
Safety data on specific peptide serums are limited. Eye-area products carry general irritation risks, and prescription bimatoprost has documented effects such as redness and eyelid darkening.

angle.text: Users apply these drug-free serums along the lash line hoping for longer, thicker lashes that frame the eyes and make them look fuller and more defined. They are sold as alternatives to prescription prostaglandin products. Trials exist for prescription bimatoprost, not for the peptide versions.

lead: Over-the-counter eyelash growth serums are cosmetic liquids or gels applied along the lash line with the aim of making eyelashes look longer, thicker or fuller. Many are marketed as drug-free alternatives to prescription prostaglandin products, and typically list peptides, conditioning agents, botanical extracts or vitamins as their active ingredients rather than a prostaglandin analogue.[1][2]

Lashes behave differently from scalp hair: according to Wikipedia, their length is largely genetically set, the number of follicles cannot increase after birth, and length, thickness and darkness decline with age.[1] The same article notes that some cosmetic brands use peptides instead of prostaglandins because of regulatory rules in places such as Canada and California.[1]

No published human trial of a peptide-based lash serum was identified in the research used for this article, so claims about their effect rest on manufacturer statements and user reports. On looksmax.org the products are discussed alongside prescription bimatoprost (Latisse), castor oil, rosemary oil and minoxidil.
infobox: Liquid or gel applied with a brush to the lash line

paras: Peptide lash serums are sold by many cosmetic brands. Manufacturers describe the products as supporting lash health or the appearance of lash length and density. Some products are water-based, which forum users note feels different from oil-based remedies when applied.

Latisse (bimatoprost) is a prostaglandin analogue and, per Wikipedia, was the first drug approved by the FDA for eyelash growth, introduced in 2009. Noticeable growth takes up to about 16 weeks, mainly on the upper lashes, with reported length increases of up to 25%.[1] Bimatoprost is also approved for glaucoma and ocular hypertension; its reported adverse effects include eye redness, eyelid darkening and, with the eye-drop use, permanent iris darkening.[2] Peptide serums are a separate product category and these figures do not describe them.
No studies found. Published trial data on lash growth relate mainly to prostaglandin analogues such as bimatoprost, which are a different class of product.[1][2]

Threads on looksmax.org ask which lash serum to use and whether results are visible. One user who had used castor oil for a month reported that lashes looked healthier but not thicker and asked about serums; a reply suggested Latisse. Another thread asks whether a water-based serum from a mass-market skincare brand works, with the poster comparing it to rosemary oil they said felt more saturating. Other threads compare lash serums with oral minoxidil, and one reply says topical minoxidil is not recommended for lashes.

lore.intro: In forum discussion, lash serums are treated as a milder or more accessible option than prescription bimatoprost, with mixed reports of results.

claims.claim: Lash serums can make lashes visibly thicker
Minoxidil can be combined with or substituted for lash serum
Oils such as castor or rosemary oil work like serums

timeline.event: Latisse (bimatoprost) introduced as the first FDA-approved drug for eyelash growth.[1]
